title: THE SUCCESS THAT COMES FROM ENVY
paragraphs: THE SUCCESS THAT COMES FROM ENVY
Understanding the Deep Meaning of Ecclesiastes 4:4
There is a kind of success that looks beautiful from a distance but feels empty when you finally touch it.
It earns applause.
It attracts attention.
It creates admiration.

But underneath the polished image, the expensive lifestyle, the growing numbers, the promotions, the achievements, and the endless pursuit of more, there can be something surprisingly dark driving the entire journey.
King Solomon saw it thousands of years ago.
And what he observed may be even more relevant today than when he first wrote it.
Ecclesiastes 4:4 says:
“Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.” (ESV)
The Hebrew text is striking:
וְרָאִיתִי אֲנִי אֶת־כָּל־עָמָל וְאֵת כָּל־כִּשְׁרוֹן הַמַּעֲשֶׂה כִּי הִיא קִנְאַת־אִישׁ מֵרֵעֵהוּ
Transliterated:
Ve-ra'iti ani et kol amal ve'et kol kishron hama'aseh ki hi qin'at ish mere'ehu.
Several words deserve careful attention.
The word עָמָל (amal) refers to labor, toil, exhausting effort, and burdensome work.
The word כִּשְׁרוֹן (kishron) refers to skill, excellence, achievement, competence, and success.
The word קִנְאָה (qin'ah) means jealousy, envy, rivalry, or competitive zeal.
Solomon is not saying every successful person is envious.
He is saying that after observing human society, he noticed how much labor and achievement are fueled by comparison with others.
He looked beneath the surface.
He examined motives.
He watched the human heart.
And what he discovered was uncomfortable.
Many people are not running toward a calling.
They are running away from feeling inferior.
Many people are not pursuing purpose.
They are pursuing superiority.
Many people do not want success because God called them to it.
They want success because someone else already has it.
That distinction changes everything.
The Hidden Engine Behind Modern Success
The world celebrates ambition.
Work harder.
Build bigger.
Earn more.
Grow faster.
Outperform everyone.
Beat the competition.
Become unforgettable.
But Scripture repeatedly warns that the human heart is capable of disguising sinful motives beneath admirable accomplishments.
A promotion can be driven by stewardship.
Or it can be driven by envy.
A business can be built to glorify God.
Or it can be built to make someone else jealous.
A ministry can grow through genuine obedience.
Or it can grow through competition with another ministry.
Outwardly, the results may look identical.
Only God sees the motive.
The Apostle Paul understood this reality.
In Philippians 1:15, he wrote:
“Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will.”
Even ministry itself can become infected by envy.
That should humble all of us.
The Human Story Nobody Wants to Admit
Social media has amplified what Solomon observed.
Every scroll presents another opportunity to compare.
Someone is wealthier.
Someone is younger.
Someone is more successful.
Someone is more attractive.
Someone appears happier.
Someone's marriage seems stronger.
Someone's ministry seems larger.
Someone's business seems more profitable.
Comparison has become one of the most consumed products in human history.
And envy rarely introduces itself honestly.
It does not say:
"I want what God has assigned to me."
It says:
"I want what God gave them."
That is exactly what happened in the Garden.
The serpent convinced Eve that God was withholding something.
The temptation was not merely the fruit.
The temptation was comparison.
Someone else has what you do not.
And that seed of comparison has been growing in the human heart ever since.
The Exhaustion of Chasing Someone Else's Life
Solomon describes envy-driven success as "vanity."
The Hebrew word is הֶבֶל (hevel).
It literally means vapor.
Mist.
Breath.
Something temporary and impossible to grasp.
Imagine trying to capture smoke with your hands.
That is the picture Solomon paints.
Envy promises satisfaction.
But once you reach the goal, satisfaction evaporates.
The house becomes normal.
The salary becomes expected.
The recognition fades.
The achievement loses its power.
Then comparison finds another target.
Someone else is still ahead.
Someone else still has more.
Someone else still appears better.
The race never ends because envy never allows contentment.
That is why Solomon also calls it:
"רְעוּת רוּחַ"
Re'ut Ruach.
A striving after wind.
Chasing the wind is exhausting because the wind can never be possessed.
And comparison works the same way.
No matter how much you gain, someone always has more.
The Gospel's Radical Alternative
Jesus offers something completely different.
The world says:
"Become more than everyone else."
Jesus says:
"Follow Me."
The world says:
"Prove yourself."
Jesus says:
"It is finished."
The world says:
"Your value comes from outperforming others."
Jesus says:
"You are loved because of My grace."
The cross destroys the entire comparison game.
At Calvary, every human being stands equally needy.
The wealthy need grace.
The poor need grace.
The famous need grace.
The forgotten need grace.
The successful need grace.
The failures need grace.
Nobody earns salvation through achievement.
Nobody climbs high enough to deserve redemption.
The ground is level at the foot of the cross.
This is why the Gospel is so liberating.
You no longer have to compete for your worth.
Your identity is found in Christ.
You no longer have to measure your life against your neighbor.
God has written a unique calling for you.
You no longer have to envy someone else's story.
Because Jesus is writing your own.
From Comparison to Calling
There is a profound difference between ambition and envy.
Biblical ambition says:
"Lord, help me maximize what You have entrusted to me."
Envy says:
"Lord, why didn't You give me what You entrusted to them?"
Biblical ambition produces gratitude.
Envy produces resentment.
Biblical ambition celebrates others.
Envy secretly hopes they fail.
Biblical ambition glorifies God.
Envy glorifies self.
One leads to peace.
The other leads to exhaustion.
The scandal of the human condition is not merely that we sin.
It is that we often build entire lives around motives we refuse to acknowledge.
Yet this is where grace enters the story.
Jesus does not merely forgive our actions.
He transforms our hearts.
He exposes the envy we hide.
He heals the insecurity beneath it.
He teaches us contentment.
He frees us from comparison.
And He invites us into something far greater than competing with our neighbors.
He invites us to walk with Him.
Perhaps that is why Ecclesiastes remains so powerful.
Solomon looked at the trophies of humanity and saw what many refuse to see.
Success itself is not the problem.
The heart behind it is.
A life fueled by envy will eventually leave a person empty.
A life surrendered to Christ will ultimately leave a person fulfilled.
One chases the wind.
The other follows the Savior.
And only one of those journeys leads home.
Maybe as you read this, the Holy Spirit is gently revealing places where comparison has quietly taken root.
Not to condemn you.
But to free you.
Because Jesus did not die so you could spend your life chasing someone else's blessing.
He died so you could become who God created you to be.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
That is the power of grace.
That is the hope found in Christ.
And that is why every story can change.
If this message stirred something in your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Be honest.
Have you ever found yourself chasing something simply because someone else had it?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is fighting the same battle.
The most dangerous chains are often the ones we mistake for motivation.
